spark.title: How to Prepare for High-Level Design (HLD)
spark.summary: Master the 45-minute HLD interview using the RESHADED framework: scope requirements, estimate QPS/storage, design APIs and data models, and deep-dive into bottlenecks and failure modes.
spark.keyTakeaway: If latency budgets leave no room for synchronous retries, lead the conversation with structured milestones—never jump straight to drawing boxes before locking down functional scope, scale numbers, and read/write ratios.
spark.byteSummary:
Master the 45-minute HLD interview using the RESHADED framework: scope requirements, estimate QPS/storage, design APIs and data models, and deep-dive into bottlenecks and failure modes.

Most HLD interviews fail in the first 10 minutes—not from lack of distributed systems knowledge, but from designing the wrong system at the wrong scale.

Lead the conversation with structured milestones—never jump straight to drawing boxes before locking down functional scope, scale numbers, and read/write ratios.

concept.whyItMatters: Most HLD interviews fail in the first 10 minutes—not from lack of distributed systems knowledge, but from designing the wrong system at the wrong scale. Using a repeatable framework ([Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation](/concept/back-of-the-envelope-estimation) + [CAP/Consistency](/concept/cap-theorem-consistency-models) + bottleneck deep dives) keeps you driving the 45-minute session like a Staff/Principal engineer.
whenToUse: 45–60 minute Senior/Staff/Principal High-Level Design rounds (e.g., Design a Rate Limiter, URL Shortener, Payment Ledger, or Notification Engine).
Structuring open-ended architecture reviews with explicit trade-off matrices.
whenNotToUse: Spending 20 minutes on boilerplate auth/login flows instead of the core scaling bottleneck.
keyPoints: Minutes 0–5 (Requirements & Scope): Lock 3–4 core functional requirements and 2–3 non-functional SLOs (availability, p99 latency, consistency).
Minutes 5–10 (Estimation): Compute average QPS, peak QPS (3x), daily/5-year storage, and cache RAM using powers of 2.
Minutes 10–25 (Core API & High-Level Architecture): Define clean REST/gRPC contracts, storage schema ([SQL vs. NoSQL](/concept/sql-vs-nosql-tradeoffs)), and end-to-end read/write paths.

Minutes 25–45 (Deep Dives & Failure Modes): Address hot keys, [sharding](/concept/database-sharding), [idempotency](/concept/idempotency-and-deduplication), [backpressure](/concept/backpressure-flow-control), and multi-AZ failover.

sections.content:
## Preparation & Execution Matrix

| Timebox | Stage | Key Questions to Answer |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **0–5m** | Requirements | Who are the users? Read/write ratio? Consistency vs. availability? |
| **5–10m** | Capacity Math | Avg/Peak QPS? 5-yr storage? Hot-set RAM? |
| **10–25m** | HLD & Schema | Core endpoints, DB choice, partition key, caching layer |
| **25–45m** | Deep Dive | Hot-partition mitigation, replication lag, DLQ, observability |

## Reference Templates (Python & Java)

```python
# 45-minute HLD pacing checklist helper (Python)
HLD_STEPS = [
    ("0-5m", "Clarify functional & non-functional SLOs"),
    ("5-10m", "Compute QPS, Peak QPS (3x), 5-yr storage, RAM"),
    ("10-25m", "Define APIs, DB schema, and end-to-end data flow"),
    ("25-45m", "Deep-dive bottlenecks, sharding, caching, and failures"),
]
```

```java
// 45-minute HLD pacing checklist (Java)
List<String> hldStages = List.of(
    "0-5m: Scope & SLOs",
    "5-10m: Capacity & QPS math",
    "10-25m: APIs, Schema & HLD",
    "25-45m: Bottlenecks & Failure Modes"
);
```

simulation.title: How To Prepare For Hld — Interactive Execution Walkthrough

steps.title: Normal Request Path
steps.explanation: Caller sends work into the gateway with explicit timeout and concurrency bounds (Normal Request Path).

steps.title: Contention & Load Spike
steps.explanation: The core engine processes the hot path while keeping state transitions deterministic (Contention & Load Spike).

steps.title: Partial Failure Mode
steps.explanation: Under load or replica lag, bounded backoff and isolation prevent cascading saturation (Partial Failure Mode).

steps.title: Convergence & Recovery
steps.explanation: State converges cleanly and telemetry confirms the system returned within its SLO envelope (Convergence & Recovery).

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement How To Prepare For Hld without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: If latency budgets leave no room for synchronous retries, lead the conversation with structured milestones—never jump straight to drawing boxes before locking down functional scope, scale numbers, and read/write ratios.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

decisionExercise.prompt: When How To Prepare For Hld experiences a sudden 5x traffic spike alongside a slow downstream dependency, which engineering choice best protects system stability?

options.label: Increase retry counts and remove client timeouts so every request eventually succeeds.
options.explanation: Unbounded retries multiply load on an already struggling dependency and exhaust worker pools.

options.label: Enforce strict latency budgets, bounded jittered retries, and graceful fallback or load shedding.
options.explanation: Bounding retries and isolating slow paths preserves healthy capacity and keeps tail latency predictable.
